sentences.t: Кая раны дорога, братіе, забывъ чти и живота, и града Чрънигова, отня злата стола, и своя милыя хоти красныя Глѣбовны свычая и обычая?
sentences.tr: Kaja rany doroga, bratie, zabyvŭ čti i života, i grada Črŭnigova, otnja zlata stola, i svoja milyja xoti krasnyja Glěbovny svyčaja i obyčaja?
sentences.l: What wound is [so] dear, brothers, [that one would go] forgetting honor and life, and the city of Chernigov, [his] father's golden throne, and his own dear beloved, fair Glebovna's sweet ways and habits?
sentences.i: What old wound, brothers, is so precious that a man forgets honor and life, the city of Chernigov, his father's golden throne, and the sweet ways of his own dear, fair Glebovna?
sentences.n: The opening question of this movement, generally read as directed at Oleg Svyatoslavich (the whole excursus that follows is about him): what past grievance could be dear enough to make a prince give up honor, life, the city of Chernigov, and his father's golden throne — and the company of his beloved? The syntax of «Кая раны дорога» is itself debated (a rare use of the interrogative кая with a genitive complement, 'what of a wound', rather than a plain agreeing adjective); we keep the printed wording. хоть is an old noun for 'beloved, wife' (not related to modern 'хоть' = 'though'). «Глѣбовны», 'daughter of Gleb' — presumably Oleg's own beloved or wife — is otherwise unattested outside this poem; we do not claim a firmer identity than survives. «отня злата стола» ('father's golden throne') anchors the excursus to Chernigov, the patrimony of Oleg's father Svyatoslav Yaroslavich, over which Oleg spent much of his life fighting his cousins.

sentences.t: Были вѣчи Трояни, минула лѣта Ярославля; были плъци Олговы, Ольга Святьславличя.
sentences.tr: Byli věči Trojani, minula lěta Jaroslavlja; byli plŭci Olgovy, Olĭga Svjatĭslavličja.
sentences.l: There were the ages of Troyan, past are the years of Yaroslav; there were the wars of Oleg, of Oleg Svyatoslavich.
sentences.i: The ages of Troyan have come and gone; the years of Yaroslav have passed; there were the wars of Oleg — Oleg, son of Svyatoslav.
sentences.n: «вѣчи Трояни», 'the ages of Troyan,' echoes part 1's obscure «тропу Трояню» ('Troyan's trail') — whether Troyan is a pagan god, the Roman emperor Trajan remembered in half-legendary form, or simply a personified 'olden time,' is genuinely unresolved, and we leave the name untranslated as elsewhere. «лѣта Ярославля» are the years of Yaroslav the Wise (d. 1054), remembered here as a vanished, more settled era. This sentence pivots from that distant, half-legendary past to the wars of Oleg Svyatoslavich (d. 1115) — Igor's own grandfather — that the rest of this movement recounts; были/минула, simple past forms, mark all three eras as closed and gone.

sentences.t: Тъй бо Олегъ мечемъ крамолу коваше, и стрѣлы по земли сѣяше. Ступаетъ въ златъ стремень въ градѣ Тьмутороканѣ.
sentences.tr: Tŭj bo Olegŭ mečemŭ kramolu kovaše, i strěly po zemli sějaše. Stupajetŭ vŭ zlatŭ stremenĭ vŭ gradě Tĭmutorokaně.
sentences.l: For that Oleg forged strife with the sword, and sowed arrows across the land. He steps into the golden stirrup in the city of Tmutorokan.
sentences.i: For that same Oleg forged strife with his sword, and sowed arrows across the land. He sets his foot in the golden stirrup in the city of Tmutorokan.
sentences.n: коваше and сѣяше are imperfects — a habitual, repeated past ('kept forging,' 'kept sowing'), fitting a whole career of warfare rather than one act. «мечемъ крамолу коваше», 'forged strife with the sword,' and «стрѣлы по земли сѣяше», 'sowed arrows across the land,' both turn peaceful craft-and-farming verbs (to forge, to sow) into images of war — the sowing image returns later in this same part, when bones are 'sown' on the battlefield. «Ступаетъ» is a vivid historic present. Tmutorokan (Тьмуторокань), the Rus' principality on the Taman peninsula, became Oleg's own base after his return from Byzantine exile around 1083; from there he repeatedly fought, often with Polovtsian allies, for Chernigov and a share of power in Rus'. The 'golden stirrup' formula deliberately echoes part 1's «въступи Игорь Князь въ златъ стремень» for Igor's own setting-out — the poet mirrors grandfather and grandson.

sentences.t: Тоже звонъ слыша давный великый Ярославь сынъ Всеволожь: а Владиміръ по вся утра уши закладаше въ Черниговѣ;
sentences.tr: Tože zvonŭ slyša davnyj velikyj Jaroslavĭ synŭ Vsevoložĭ: a Vladimirŭ po vsja utra uši zakladaše vŭ Černigově;
sentences.l: That same clang the great, long-ago Yaroslav, son of Vsevolod, heard: and Vladimir, every morning, stopped up his ears in Chernigov;
sentences.i: That same clang the great old Yaroslav, son of Vsevolod, once heard — while Vladimir, morning after morning, stopped his ears in Chernigov;
sentences.n: A genuine crux. As printed, «Ярославь сынъ Всеволожь» reads 'Yaroslav, son of Vsevolod' — but no prince of that description fits the date, while the very next clause names 'Vladimir,' almost certainly Vladimir Monomakh (d. 1125), who really was the son of Vsevolod Yaroslavich (Grand Prince of Kiev, 1078–93). Many editors therefore suspect the name and patronymic have been transposed in transmission and that the sense is 'Vsevolod, son of Yaroslav' — Vsevolod Yaroslavich himself, hearing the same old alarm his own son later lived with; we keep the 1800 word order and flag the doubt rather than silently emending it. Vladimir Monomakh held the princely seat of Chernigov from 1078 until 1094, when, after prolonged Polovtsian-backed pressure from Oleg, he ceded the city to him — an episode Monomakh himself describes in his Instruction (Поучение). «по вся утра уши закладаше», 'stopped his ears every morning,' is usually read figuratively, for enduring the daily alarm and violence of Oleg's assault on the city.

sentences.t: Бориса же Вячеславлича слава на судъ приведе, и на канину зелену паполому постла, за обиду Олгову храбра и млада Князя.
sentences.tr: Borisa že Vjačeslavliča slava na sudŭ privede, i na kaninu zelenu papolomu postla, za obidu Olgovu xrabra i mlada Knjazja.
sentences.l: But Boris Vyacheslavich, glory brought to judgment, and on green Kanina spread [him as] a pall, for the insult to Oleg — brave and young prince.
sentences.i: But as for Boris Vyacheslavich — glory led him to his reckoning, and laid him out on a green pall at Kanina, for the wrong done to Oleg, that brave young prince.
sentences.n: Boris Vyacheslavich, grandson of Yaroslav the Wise through his son Vyacheslav, allied with Oleg Svyatoslavich to fight for Chernigov against Vsevolod Yaroslavich and Izyaslav Yaroslavich; he was killed at the Battle of Nezhatina Niva near Chernigov on 3 October 1078, an event recorded in the Primary Chronicle. «слава на судъ приведе», 'glory brought him to judgment,' reads his death as the price of the very glory he sought. «канину», 'Kanina,' is otherwise unattested; its exact location is uncertain, probably a stream or place near the battlefield, and we do not assert an identification beyond that. «паполома» is a rich pall or shroud-cloth — the same word recurs at Svyatoslav's ominous dream later in the poem. «храбра и млада Князя» ('brave and young prince') is in apposition to Oleg, tying Boris's death to the wrong Oleg had suffered — his exclusion from his patrimony — which occasioned the whole war.

sentences.t: Съ тояже Каялы Святоплъкь повелѣя отца своего междю Угорьскими иноходьцы ко Святѣй Софіи къ Кіеву.
sentences.tr: Sŭ tojaže Kajaly Svjatoplŭkĭ povelěja otca svojego meždju Ugorĭskimi inoxodĭcy ko Svjatěj Sofii kŭ Kievu.
sentences.l: From that same Kayala Svyatopolk had his father conveyed, between Hungarian ambling-horses, to Saint Sophia, to Kiev.
sentences.i: From that same Kayala, Svyatopolk had his father borne home between Hungarian ambling-horses, to St. Sophia in Kiev.
sentences.n: Svyatopolk — later Svyatopolk II Izyaslavich, Grand Prince of Kiev 1093–1113 — was son of Izyaslav Yaroslavich, Grand Prince of Kiev, who was killed fighting alongside Vsevolod against Oleg and Boris at that same 1078 battle; the chronicles record Izyaslav's body carried to Kiev and buried at St. Sophia. «иноходьцы», ambling-horses, is a smooth-gaited breed suited to carrying a body with dignity; 'Hungarian' marks them as imported, prestige animals. The real puzzle is «тояже Каялы», 'that same Kayala': the Kayala is elsewhere the river of Igor's own disaster of 1185, decades later, and no source otherwise ties any river by that name to the 1078 battle, which the chronicles place at Nezhatina Niva. Whether the poet is deliberately naming both catastrophes with one symbolic river, or the text here is corrupt, compressed, or telescoping two memories into one, is genuinely unresolved, and we do not resolve it. «повелѣя» is itself an unusual, imprecisely understood form, rendered here approximately as 'had [him] conveyed.'

sentences.t: Тогда при Олзѣ Гориславличи сѣяшется и растяшеть усобицами; погибашеть жизнь Даждь-Божа внука, въ Княжихъ крамолахъ вѣци человѣкомь скратишась.
sentences.tr: Togda pri Olzě Gorislavliči sějašetsja i rastjašetĭ usobicami; pogibašetĭ žiznĭ Daždĭ-Boža vnuka, vŭ Knjažixŭ kramolaxŭ věci čelověkomĭ skratišasĭ.
sentences.l: Then, under Oleg Gorislavich, [strife] was sown and grew with feuds; the life of Dazhbog's grandson perished, in princely quarrels the ages of men were cut short.
sentences.i: In the days of Oleg Gorislavich, strife was sown and grew with feud after feud; the life of Dazhbog's grandson perished — men's very lifetimes were cut short in the princes' quarrels.
sentences.n: «Гориславличи», 'Gorislavich,' is the poet's own bitter coinage for Oleg — a mock-patronymic built on горе, 'grief, woe,' punning on his real patronymic Svyatoslavich; it has become his standard epithet in scholarship on the poem. «Даждь-Божа внука», 'Dazhbog's grandson,' is a collective epithet for the people (and princes) of Rus' as descendants of Dazhbog, the pagan sun-god named among the idols Prince Vladimir raised over Kiev before the Baptism of 988; the same figure recurs in part 4. сѣяшется, растяшеть, погибашеть are all imperfects — a sustained, ongoing past, unlike the aorists used for single completed acts elsewhere in this excursus — marking the strife as something that went on and on. вѣкъ (вѣци) here means a human lifetime, not 'century' or 'age' in the historical sense.

sentences.t: Тогда по Руской земли рѣтко ратаевѣ кикахуть: нъ часто врани граяхуть, трупіа себѣ дѣляче; а галици свою рѣчь говоряхуть, хотять полетѣти на уедіе.
sentences.tr: Togda po Ruskoj zemli rětko rataevě kikaxutĭ: nŭ často vrani grajaxutĭ, trupia sebě děljače; a galici svoju rěčĭ govorjaxutĭ, xotjatĭ poletěti na uedie.
sentences.l: Then across the Russian land rarely did the plowmen call out; but often did the ravens caw, dividing corpses among themselves; and the jackdaws spoke their own speech, wanting to fly to the carrion.
sentences.i: Then, across the land of Rus', rarely did the plowmen call to one another — but often the ravens cawed, sharing out the corpses, and the jackdaws chattered in their own tongue, eager to fly down to the feast.
sentences.n: A grim inversion of peaceful, working sounds: the plowmen's calls give way to the carrion-birds' noise. «ратаевѣ» is nominative plural of ратай, 'plowman' — an old -еве/-ove type plural (rather than the -и a modern-Russian reader would expect). «дѣляче» is a present active participle, 'dividing, sharing out,' agreeing with врани. «уедіе» is a rare word for carrion, food, prey, found mainly in this poem. All three imperfects (кикахуть, граяхуть, говоряхуть) paint a habitual, ongoing wartime landscape rather than a single moment — the plowman's absence and the birds' constant noise as the new normal of the old usobitsy.

sentences.t: То было въ ты рати, и въ ты плъкы; а сице и рати не слышано:
sentences.tr: To bylo vŭ ty rati, i vŭ ty plŭky; a sice i rati ne slyšano:
sentences.l: That was in those wars, and in those campaigns; but of a war like this one nothing has been heard:
sentences.i: All that happened in those old wars, those old campaigns — but of fighting like this, nothing has ever been heard:
sentences.n: The poet's pivot: having recalled the older civil wars of Oleg's generation, he now turns back to Igor's own catastrophe and insists it surpasses even those. «ты» is the old demonstrative plural ('those'; cf. modern 'те'). «сице» = 'such, like this' (adverb); «не слышано» is an impersonal past passive ('it has not been heard'), a subjectless construction a modern-Russian reader would recast with 'никто не слышал.' This sentence introduces the description of the second day's battle that follows — echoing, in miniature, the poem's larger claim that Igor's defeat outdoes every earlier disaster it recalls.

sentences.t: съ зараніа до вечера, съ вечера до свѣта летятъ стрѣлы каленыя; гримлютъ сабли о шеломы; трещатъ копіа харалужныя, въ полѣ незнаемѣ среди земли Половецкыи.
sentences.tr: sŭ zarania do večera, sŭ večera do světa letjatŭ strěly kalenyja; grimljutŭ sabli o šelomy; treščatŭ kopia xaralužnyja, vŭ polě neznaemě sredi zemli Poloveckyi.
sentences.l: from morning to evening, from evening to daylight fly tempered arrows; sabers clang on helmets; kharalug spears crack, in the unknown field, in the midst of the Polovtsian land.
sentences.i: From dawn to dusk, from dusk to daybreak, tempered arrows fly; sabers ring against helmets; spears of kharalug steel crack and splinter — in an unknown field, in the heart of the Polovtsian land.
sentences.n: A tight triad of present-tense verbs (летятъ, гримлютъ, трещатъ) compresses two days and a night of fighting into one continuous, timeless present. «каленыя» = 'tempered [by fire]', of arrows. «харалужныя» names the same legendary hard steel used of Vsevolod's blades in part 2; its exact origin (possibly a Turkic loanword) is debated, but it consistently marks superior weapons throughout the poem. «незнаемѣ» ('unknown') echoes part 1's and part 2's language for hostile, unfamiliar ground — the poem repeatedly stresses that the Rus' are fighting deep in enemy territory, far from home.

sentences.t: Чръна земля подъ копыты, костьми была посѣяна, а кровію польяна; тугою взыдоша по Руской земли.
sentences.tr: Črŭna zemlja podŭ kopyty, kostĭmi byla posějana, a kroviju polĭjana; tugoju vzydoša po Ruskoj zemli.
sentences.l: Black earth under hooves was sown with bones, and watered with blood; with sorrow [they] sprang up across the Russian land.
sentences.i: Black earth beneath the hooves was sown with bones and watered with blood — and grief sprang up like a harvest across the land of Rus'.
sentences.n: The poem's grimmest sowing-image: bones stand for seed, blood for the water that makes seed grow, and взыдоша (literally 'sprang, sprouted up') figures grief as the resulting harvest — completing the image begun earlier in this part with Oleg's 'sowing of arrows.' The precise grammatical subject of взыдоша (aorist 3pl, 'they sprang up') is not spelled out; we take it, as most readers do, to continue the harvest metaphor (grief 'sprouting' where the bones were sown) rather than naming a literal subject. была посѣяна / была ... польяна use the periphrastic passive (быти + past passive participle) exactly as modern Russian still does ('была посеяна'); note only that была is not repeated before польяна, carried over by ellipsis from the first clause.

sentences.t: Что ми шумить, что ми звенить давечя рано предъ зорями? Игорь плъкы заворочаетъ; жаль бо ему мила брата Всеволода.
sentences.tr: Čto mi šumitĭ, čto mi zvenitĭ davečja rano predŭ zorjami? Igorĭ plŭky zavoročajetŭ; žalĭ bo jemu mila brata Vsevoloda.
sentences.l: What rustles for me, what rings for me, early just now before the dawns? Igor turns back [his] regiments; for he grieves for his dear brother Vsevolod.
sentences.i: What is that rustling, that ringing I hear, so early, before the dawns? It is Igor wheeling his regiments about — grieving for his dear brother Vsevolod.
sentences.n: A riddle the poet poses and then answers himself, the same device used of Boyan's falcons-and-swans in the proem. «ми» is an ethical dative ('to/for me'), drawing the poet — and the listener — directly into the scene. «зорями» (instr. pl., 'dawns') is plural — most likely because the fighting has by now run past more than one daybreak, though a generic poetic plural ('at the dawns,' without counting them) cannot be ruled out. «заворочаетъ» (present, 'turns back, wheels around') marks Igor trying to regroup with or rescue his hard-pressed brother's force — the hinge toward the defeat that follows. «жаль» governs the dative (ему) and genitive (мила брата Всеволода): 'it is a grief to him, for his dear brother.'

sentences.t: Бишася день, бишася другый: третьяго дни къ полуднію падоша стязи Игоревы. Ту ся брата разлучиста на брезѣ быстрой Каялы.
sentences.tr: Bišasja denĭ, bišasja drugyj: tretĭjago dni kŭ poludniju padoša stjazi Igorevy. Tu sja brata razlučista na brezě bystroj Kajaly.
sentences.l: They fought a day, they fought a second: on the third day toward noon Igor's banners fell. There the two brothers were parted on the bank of the swift Kayala.
sentences.i: They fought one day, they fought a second — on the third day, toward noon, Igor's banners went down. There the two brothers were torn apart on the bank of the swift Kayala.
sentences.n: «падоша стязи» ('the banners fell') is the poem's understated way of marking the rout and Igor's capture. «разлучиста» is a true dual verb form (3rd dual aorist reflexive of разлучити, 'to part, separate'), agreeing with «брата», itself a dual noun meaning 'the two brothers' (Igor and Vsevolod) rather than a plural — the same dual number met in part 1 for the two brothers' speech ('оба есвѣ'), lost entirely in modern Russian. The Kayala, the river of the whole disaster, remains unidentified with any known watercourse.

sentences.t: Ту кроваваго вина недоста; ту пиръ докончаша храбріи Русичи: сваты попоиша, а сами полегоша за землю Рускую.
sentences.tr: Tu krovavago vina nedosta; tu pirŭ dokončaša xrabrii Rusiči: svaty popoiša, a sami polegoša za zemlju Ruskuju.
sentences.l: There bloody wine ran short; there the brave men of Rus' finished the feast: they gave the in-laws to drink, and themselves lay down for the Russian land.
sentences.i: There the bloody wine ran out; there the brave sons of Rus' finished the feast — they poured out drink for their in-laws, and lay down themselves for the land of Rus'.
sentences.n: The poem's most famous battle-as-feast conceit closes this movement: blood figures as 'wine,' the slaughter as a 'feast' the Rus' warriors 'finish' (докончаша), and death itself as simply 'lying down' (полегоша), a common Old Rus' euphemism for dying in battle also found in the chronicles. «сваты», literally 'matchmakers, in-laws,' addresses the Polovtsians with bitter irony: Rus' princes and Polovtsian khans regularly sealed truces with marriages (Igor's own son Vladimir later married a daughter of Khan Konchak), so the poem casts the massacre itself as a poisoned wedding-feast, the 'in-laws' served death instead of the toasts of kinship. недоста is an impersonal aorist ('was lacking, ran short'), governing the genitive object «кроваваго вина».

glossary.до: до — up to, as far as (prep. + gen.)
glossary.за: за — for, for the sake of; behind, beyond (prep.)
glossary.своя: свой — his own (sg. fem., agreeing with 'хоти')
glossary.русичи: Русичь — the men of Rus' (nom. pl.)
glossary.ольга: Олегъ — Oleg's (gen. sg.); Igor's grandfather Oleg Svyatoslavich
glossary.зараніа: заранье — early morning (gen. sg., 'from early morning')
glossary.кая: кыи — what, which (interrog. pron., fem. sg.; 'what kind of')
glossary.дорога: дорогъ — dear, precious (short-form adj., fem. sg., predicate)
glossary.забывъ: забыти — having forgotten (past active participle / gerund)
glossary.чрънигова: Чрьниговъ — Chernigov (gen. sg.); a city, the seat of Oleg's line
glossary.стола: столъ — throne, seat (gen. sg.; lit. 'seat, chair')
glossary.хоти: хоть — beloved, wife (gen. sg.; an old noun for a loved one)
glossary.глѣбовны: Глѣбовна — daughter of Gleb (gen. sg.); apparently Oleg Svyatoslavich's beloved, otherwise unidentified
glossary.свычая: свычай — habit, familiar way (gen. sg.; paired with обычай in the old doublet 'свычаи и обычаи')
glossary.трояни: Троянь — Troyan's (possessive adj., nom. pl.); an obscure mythic/historical name, as in part 1
glossary.ярославля: Ярославль — Yaroslav's (possessive adj., neut. pl., agreeing with 'лѣта'); Yaroslav the Wise (d. 1054)
glossary.олговы: Ольговъ — Oleg's (possessive adj., nom. pl.); Oleg Svyatoslavich, Igor's grandfather
glossary.святьславличя: Святьславличь — Svyatoslavich's, son of Svyatoslav's (gen. sg.); Oleg's patronymic
glossary.тъй: тъй — that, this (dem. pron., nom. sg. masc.)
glossary.олегъ: Олегъ — Oleg (nom. sg.); Oleg Svyatoslavich (d. 1115), Igor's grandfather, called 'Gorislavich' later in this part
glossary.земли: земля — land (loc./dat. sg., 'over/across the land'; also gen. sg. after 'среди')
glossary.тьмутороканѣ: Тьмуторокань — Tmutorokan (loc. sg.); Rus' principality on the Taman peninsula, Oleg's power base
glossary.ярославь: Ярославль — Yaroslav (nom. sg.); as printed 'Yaroslav, son of Vsevolod' — probably a transposed reference to Vsevolod Yaroslavich (see note)
glossary.всеволожь: Всеволожь — Vsevolod's (possessive adj., nom. sg. masc.)
glossary.владиміръ: Владиміръ — Vladimir (nom. sg.); almost certainly Vladimir Monomakh (d. 1125)
glossary.вся: весь — every, all (acc. pl. neut., 'по вся утра' = 'every morning')
glossary.бориса: Борисъ — Boris (acc. sg.); Boris Vyacheslavich, killed 1078 at Nezhatina Niva
glossary.вячеславлича: Вячеславличь — Vyacheslavich, son of Vyacheslav (acc. sg.); patronymic
glossary.канину: Канина — Kanina (acc. sg.); an otherwise unidentified place, probably near the 1078 battlefield
glossary.олгову: Ольговъ — Oleg's (possessive adj., acc. sg. fem., agreeing with обиду)
glossary.храбра: храбръ — brave (gen. sg. masc., agreeing with Князя; in apposition to Oleg, understood genitivally via the possessive adj. Олгову)
glossary.млада: младъ — young (gen. sg. masc., agreeing with Князя; in apposition to Oleg, understood genitivally via the possessive adj. Олгову)
glossary.князя: кънязь — prince (gen. sg.; in apposition to Oleg — 'Олгову ... Князя', the possessive adjective standing for a genitive)
glossary.тояже: тъйже — that same (dem. pron., gen. sg. fem.)
glossary.каялы: Каяла — the river Kayala (gen. sg.; unidentified)
glossary.святоплъкь: Святоплъкъ — Svyatopolk (nom. sg.); Svyatopolk Izyaslavich, later Grand Prince of Kiev 1093–1113
glossary.повелѣя: — (an obscure, debated form, rendered approximately 'had [him] conveyed, ordered')
glossary.ко: къ — to, toward (prep. + dat.; form used before a consonant cluster)
glossary.софіи: Софія — Sophia (dat. sg.); St. Sophia cathedral in Kiev
glossary.при: при — in the time of, under (prep. + loc.)
glossary.олзѣ: Олегъ — Oleg (loc. sg.; 'при Олзѣ' = 'in Oleg's days')
glossary.гориславличи: Гориславличь — Gorislavich (loc. sg.); the poet's ironic epithet for Oleg, 'son of Woe' (punning on his real patronymic Svyatoslavich)
glossary.усобицами: усобица — with feuds, with internecine wars (instr. pl.)
glossary.даждь-божа: Даждьбогъ — Dazhbog's (possessive adj., gen. sg.); the pagan sun-god, an ancestor-figure of the Rus'/princes
glossary.скратишась: скратитися — were cut short, shortened (aorist 3pl, reflexive)
glossary.руской: руськый — Russian, of Rus' (loc. sg. fem., adj.)
glossary.дѣляче: дѣлити — dividing, sharing out (present active participle)
glossary.уедіе: уѣдие — carrion, prey, food (acc. sg.; rare word)
glossary.было: быти — was (impersonal past 3sg neut., 'that was so')
glossary.рати: рать — wars, campaigns (acc. pl., 'въ ты рати'; also gen. sg., 'и рати не слышано' = 'of such a campaign')
glossary.слышано: слышати — has been heard (past passive participle, impersonal)
glossary.харалужныя: харалужный — of kharalug [steel], tempered (nom. pl.); a legendary hard steel
glossary.незнаемѣ: незнаемый — unknown (loc. sg., agreeing with полѣ)
glossary.среди: среди — amid, in the midst of (prep. + gen.)
glossary.половецкыи: половецкый — Polovtsian, Cuman (gen. sg. fem., adj.)
glossary.чръна: чръный — black (nom. sg. fem., short form)
glossary.посѣяна: посѣяти — sown (past passive participle, fem. sg.)
glossary.польяна: польяти — watered, drenched (past passive participle, fem. sg.)
glossary.тугою: туга — with sorrow, with grief (instr. sg.)
glossary.ми: азъ — to me, for me (dat. sg. enclitic)
glossary.давечя: давечя — just now, a while ago (adv.)
glossary.заворочаетъ: заворочати — turns back, wheels around (3sg pres.)
glossary.жаль: жаль — (it is) a grief, a pity (impersonal predicative, + dat. + gen. object)
glossary.мила: милый — dear (gen. sg. masc., agreeing with брата)
glossary.брата: братъ — brother (gen. sg., 'for his dear brother'); also the two brothers (nom. dual, with разлучиста)
glossary.бишася: битися — fought, there was fighting (aorist, reflexive)
glossary.другый: другый — a second, the other (acc. sg. masc.)
glossary.третьяго: третий — third (gen. sg., 'третьяго дни' = 'on the third day')
glossary.игоревы: Игоревъ — Igor's (possessive adj., nom. pl., agreeing with 'стязи')
glossary.разлучиста: разлучити — were parted, separated (aorist, dual, reflexive)
glossary.брезѣ: брегъ — bank, shore (loc. sg., 'on the bank')
glossary.быстрой: быстрый — swift (gen. sg. fem., agreeing with Каялы)
glossary.недоста: недостати — was lacking, ran short (aorist 3sg, impersonal + gen.)
glossary.сваты: сватъ — matchmaker, in-law (acc. pl.); here ironically of the Polovtsians
glossary.попоиша: попоити — gave to drink, made drink (aorist 3pl)
glossary.полегоша: полечи — lay down (aorist 3pl; euphemism for 'died in battle')
glossary.рускую: руськый — Russian, of Rus' (acc. sg. fem., adj.)
